prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated without light-shift perturbation, taking optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. After the full first round I hold it for scientific reasons that I can state in atomic-physics terms, and not because six of eight of us now point the same way (the chair rightly notes that three colleagues arrived there by reading each other). The central idea is that a trapping laser normally shifts the two clock levels by different amounts, which is fatal for precision spectroscopy, but at a specially chosen wavelength the two shifts are equal and the transition frequency is left alone. Katori proposed this engineered light-shift trap and, with his group, made the first strontium lattice clock in the 2000s. Ye's group then took the system to the accuracy and stability frontier, showed that the many atoms in the lattice give statistical power, and studied the many-body and collisional physics of the lattice clock itself. Independent laboratories now reproduce uncertainties near 10^-18, and the comparisons across laboratories and fibre links agree, which is the confirmation I ask for. The consequences are things we can measure: the gravitational redshift over millimetre to centimetre heights, tighter limits on drifting constants, and searches for certain dark-matter couplings. As a theorist who has computed light shifts and polarisabilities for a living, I regard the dependence of the clock result on the quality of atomic-structure calculations (the blackbody-radiation shift, the magic wavelength itself) as a sign that the field is quantitatively under control. I answer the chair's first question as follows: the citation should be about the magic-wavelength trap and what it allows (neutral atoms, very many of them, without perturbation), and not about frequency counting (2005) or single-ion control (2012). The phrase 'at the 10^-18 level' avoids naming one record that will change.
statement.case_against: The honest objections remain the same three. First, novelty: a member who sees lattice clocks as the next step on the precision-spectroscopy ladder honoured in 2005 and 2012 will find a continuation here, and I cannot prove that reading wrong, only argue that the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate physical principle with a separate payoff (many atoms, not one ion). Second, attribution at the edges: Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Derevianko and Pal'chikov on the theory of magic wavelengths and light shifts, and the NIST ion-clock groups (Al+) are outside the credit. I should be plain about my own check, which the chair asked for: from my knowledge of the literature, Katori's proposal of the lattice with a magic wavelength (2001-2003) and the first strontium lattice clock (about 2005) come from his group, and the JILA strontium work then established the accuracy and stability record (several papers between 2006 and 2015, reaching the 10^-18 range). Derevianko and Pal'chikov calculated magic wavelengths and the associated shifts, and Lemonde's group demonstrated strontium lattice spectroscopy in parallel, but these were calculations and parallel realisations that followed, or sat alongside, the originating idea. I believe Katori and Ye is defensible, but I am recalling dates and journals from memory and I would want the committee's external experts to confirm the sequence before the final vote. Third, the SI second has not been redefined. I do not think a prize should wait for that: the discovery and its verification are complete, and the CGPM timetable is a metrology decision that is partly outside physics.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to the lattice clock, accepted that engineering the light shift is more than an application of the comb, and asked me directly whether I see any closeness to Katori or Ye, while keeping B012 as the stronger candidate if the committee wants a discovery about nature.
responses.response: I answer the direct question first: I have no collaboration, joint publication, or institutional tie to Katori or to Ye; I know their papers and have refereed or read around them as anyone in AMO would, which is knowledge and not a conflict. That is the main reason I am willing to say the physics out loud, as you asked. I also take your distinction between an instrument and a discovery seriously, and I do not think it is a sharp one here: the lattice clock is an instrument whose first results were themselves findings (the precise polarisability and blackbody shifts, collisional and many-body effects among the lattice atoms, redshift over a millimetre). If the committee chooses to look at B012 as a second prize part later, I would want the three-name question settled by experts before I vote for it, but I would not oppose it on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps IceCube (Halzen and Karle) as his first choice because it is a discovery of a clue from nature, admits that attribution is its main weakness and that source evidence stands at roughly four sigma for NGC 1068, and says my argument that magic-wavelength trapping is a real conceptual step moves B007 closer to his first place.
responses.response: I accept your criterion, which is close to my own: I prefer results where nature surprised us. The diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux is exactly such a surprise, and I have raised no doubt about it. My difficulty is the one you name yourself, that two names from a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and DUMAND behind it, would be contested, and I cannot judge that history. If you can offer a two- or three-name credit that the experts would accept, I would move B012 higher as a second part, which is why I now list it as my second alternative instead of the Hubbard-model candidate. I would not make it a one-part rival to B007 this year on a source-identification result at about four sigma, but on the diffuse flux alone I think your case is stronger than my round-1 reply, which leaned on the source evidence, suggested.

responses.point: Eriksson agrees on B007 but is cautious about B041: the Mott-superfluid transition and quantum-gas microscopy are established, but a Hubbard-model simulation that answers questions classical computers cannot is not yet shown for the fermionic case, and the four-name credit under a three-person cap is awkward.
responses.response: You are right and I have changed my second alternative because of it. In my round-1 file I ranked the cold-atom Hubbard simulator second, partly because I know the experiments well and admire them. But the defining claim of a prize in that area would be a quantitative answer that the classical methods cannot supply, and for the fermionic Hubbard model, as you say, the pseudogap and d-wave questions are still open. Four names for three places, with Cirac and Zoller overlapping with another candidate, makes the cut worse. I therefore move B041 off my alternative list. On your own pull toward B018 and B005, I defer to you and Bernhard on condensed matter, but I note again that the unresolved pairing mechanism in B005 is the opposite of the settled interpretation I would want in a companion part.

responses.point: Kroll finds atom interferometry (B043) the better companion from a measurement standpoint though the Chu question complicates credit, and wants the citation to say 'at the 10^-18 level' without naming a single record.
responses.response: I adopt your wording on the record, since the best uncertainty changes year to year, and I keep B043 as my first alternative for the reason you give: it is a precision measurement built on a clear atomic-physics principle (matter-wave interference and its sensitivity to inertial and gravitational effects). On the credit, Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich leave out Chu, and I do not think we can ignore that, so I do not propose B043 as a second part; I keep it only as an alternative if the committee wants to recognise a different part of the atomic-physics field. Where I disagree mildly is on the idea that a two-part prize is needed: with Katori and Ye as the only credited pair, a second part adds a third person at most, and I see no candidate that meets that bar this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct principle from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; this is a judgement, and I do not claim it is settled.

The exact record of 2001-2003 magic-wavelength priority and of the first strontium lattice demonstrations (Katori, JILA, Lemonde) rests on my memory and should be confirmed by external experts before the vote.
Whether a second part is useful at all: B012 has a strong discovery case but an unresolved credit, B043 has the Chu problem, B041 is not demonstrated for the fermionic case.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the SI redefinition; I would not, but a colleague who gives weight to realised impact may reasonably differ.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with the preferred B007: I have no collaboration, co-authorship or institutional link with Katori or Ye, as I confirm in answer to the chair's direct question in round 1. For the record, I collaborate closely with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and with Ursula Keller's group at ETH, so I would consider recusal if B003 (Ti:sapphire and mode-locking, crediting Keller) became a serious option; it is not part of my configuration. My collaborators Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato are not on the shortlist. B043, B041 and B012 are in or near my field or not at all, with no personal link to the credited names.
